components.text: Whether distinctive religious commitments materially worsen conflict, authoritarian politics, and public-health outcomes.
Whether religious commitments independently produce harms serious enough to defeat an overall favorable balance.
Whether religiously attributable harms establish religion's negative net effect rather than a perversion of faith.
Whether the essence of faith is punitive domination or an orientation capable of producing moral benefit.
Whether harmful doctrine should define religion as such rather than a corrupt interpretation of it.
Whether harmful conduct should be attributed to religion as such and whether removing religion improves the counterfactual world.
Whether supernatural authority is intrinsically degrading rather than capable of motivating valuable conduct.
Whether faith-based institutions produce extensive health, relief, and welfare benefits for vulnerable people.
Whether faith-based institutions make a substantial and religiously motivated contribution to health and relief.
Whether a world without religious faith would lose distinctive moral and social goods.
Whether religious health and relief provision establishes net welfare once harms caused by the same institutions are counted.
Whether the cited faith-based health and relief work establishes religion's favorable welfare contribution on balance.
Whether harmful conduct and doctrine negate the significance of faith-motivated charitable work in the overall balance.
Whether secular welfare success displaces the relevance of existing faith-motivated service.
Whether religious wrongdoing is universal or sufficiently distinctive to define religion's overall effects.
Whether religious charitable work remains probative when religious institutions also cause serious doctrinal harms.
Whether wrongdoing is sufficiently attributable and distinctive to religion to defeat its overall benefits.
Whether faith-inspired charitable work supplies a distinctively religious reason for judging religion positively overall.
Whether compassion and solidarity in faith-based service require supernatural belief or authority.
Whether authentic faith's claimed benefits distinguish religion from ordinary humanism.
Whether religion's beneficial moral and emotional content would be lost in a world without supernatural faith.
Whether compassionate institutional service is distinctively dependent on religious belief.
Whether genuine good conduct by believers establishes religion rather than ordinary human solidarity as the cause.
Whether religious compassion is merely generic humanism or is genuinely caused and organized by faith.
Whether institutional harms negate the relevance of faith-motivated aid.
Whether secular alternatives show religious aid lacks causal importance.
Whether religiously associated aid is genuinely motivated by faith or merely ordinary humanism with supernatural additions.
Whether the scale of religious aid remains materially relevant despite institutional wrongdoing.
Whether religion only deepens communal conflict or can materially help overcome divisions through its teachings and actors.
Whether faith's reconciliation role is causally real despite compassion also being available through humanism.
Whether religion necessarily deepens communal conflict rather than sometimes supplying mechanisms that overcome division.
Whether reconciliation attributed to religion is merely replaceable human compassion.
Whether religious bridge-building offsets or redeems divisions historically sustained by opposed religious identities.
Whether genuine religious motivation in beneficial conduct establishes religion's favorable net contribution.
Whether later religious peacebuilding establishes religion as a favorable causal force in communal reconciliation.
Whether authentic religious compassion and service can overcome communal divisions.
Whether religion's benefits depend on authentic faith rather than institutional arrangements.
Whether authentic religious ethics can overcome communal conflict and division.
Whether peaceful religious life depends on religion itself rather than secular institutional constraints.
Whether pluralism requires excluding religion from public participation or can combine participation with democratic limits.
Whether religious authority necessarily displaces human judgment and collective democratic authority.
Whether pluralism requires excluding religion from public participation or instead constraining all participants through democratic authority.
Whether deep faith necessarily subordinates persons to coercive authority incompatible with equal freedom.
Whether deep faith can reliably remain within democratic and equal-liberty constraints when revelation commands universal submission.
Whether coercive propagation is merely perversion or is supported by authoritative religious texts.
Whether believers can reliably remain equal democratic participants when revelation claims universal authority beyond private association.
Whether coercive religious conduct is merely a perversion rather than rooted in authoritative texts.
Whether universalizing scriptural demands are fixed and coercive or can be constrained by responsible interpretation.
Whether harmful doctrines remain insulated from correction or can be reformed through interpretive work.
Whether harmful scriptural doctrines are insulated from correction and reliably direct believers toward cruelty.
Whether authoritative texts necessarily retain coercive universal implications rather than permitting constrained interpretation.
Whether harmful literalism can be corrected through historically informed, love-centered interpretation.
Whether religious actors can help resolve sacred disputes through interfaith cooperation.
Whether abandonment of religious faith would deprive human life of awe, humility, transcendence, and moral seriousness.
Whether humane interpretation makes supernatural belief necessary for the values expressed through religion.
Whether secular availability of humility and transcendence exhausts faith's motivational contribution to moral conduct.
Whether obedience to higher power is servility or can instead be experienced as binding moral obligation.
Whether religion contributes anything motivationally distinctive when humility, awe, and morality remain available without supernatural belief.
Whether obedience to higher power is merely degrading submission rather than experienced moral obligation.
Whether admirable faith-motivated conduct establishes the truth or net goodness of religion's authority claims.
Whether good religious adherents and organized aid vindicate religious doctrine overall.
Whether examples of good believers complete the required net comparison.
Whether admirable faith-motivated service establishes that religion itself is good overall.
Whether good conduct and moral obligation among believers vindicate submission to supernatural authority.
Whether the existence of good believers resolves the motion-level causal and comparative question.
Whether repression and fanatic conformity are distinctive consequences of religion rather than broader human or ideological tendencies.
Whether religious authority uniquely creates suppression of freedom and demands for conformity.
Whether coercive universalism is confined to revealed religion.
Whether repression and demands for conformity are distinctive consequences of religious doctrine and authority.
Whether fanatical suppression is uniquely rooted in supernatural authority.
Whether coercive universalism is confined to revealed religion.
Whether the debate should exclude metaphysical meaning claims and assess only observable comparative behavior.
Whether scientific explanation and secular transcendence exhaust the rational space for religious meaning.
Whether abandoning supernatural belief leaves meaning, purpose, moral seriousness, and self-transcendence fully available.
Whether personal moral improvement can establish a broader claim about religion's goodness.
